newsitem.title: UK: Britain in new contact with Sinn Fein over talks.
newsitem.headline: Britain in new contact with Sinn Fein over talks.

text.p: Britain acknowledged on Monday it had been in contact with the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, to clarify controversial conditions for the group's eventual admission to Northern Ireland peace talks which resume on Tuesday.
Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam said her civil servants had been in touch with Sinn Fein by telephone and in writing.
The admission, after the news was broken by the Irish Times, angered Protestant unionists who said they had been misled and accused Mowlam of undermining trust in the British government.

Mowlam told a BBC Northern Ireland talk show that the contacts, broken off after an IRA double murder in June, were resumed so Sinn Fein could not blame Britain's ban on contact for the IRA's refusal to end its war against British rule.
"(British Prime Minister) Tony Blair and I have made clear all along that what's important is that Sinn Fein cannot give any excuse that we have not clarified our position", she said.

Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of a slow-moving Northern Ireland peace process, broke off exploratory talks with Sinn Fein after IRA gunmen shot dead two policeman in Lurgan in a daylight ambush whose timing and execution stunned the province.

The contacts had only just been reopened after more than a year to punish the IRA for ending a 17-month ceasefire with a London bomb that killed two and jarred peace hopes when IRA gunmen shot the two officers dead in a busy shoppers' street.
Ken Maginnis of the Ulster Unionists said the admission came after Mowlam had rejected charges in the House of Commons that contacts had been continued despite the killing.

"Very obviously, she has misled the House (of Commons). Whether that was done inadvertently...I think she has a duty to explain what went wrong," Maginis told Reuters, adding he would try to call Mowlam to parliament to explain on Tuesday.

"Unless we get an early explanation in the House of Commons then I believe the credibility of the ministerial team in the Northern Ireland office will be called into serious question and that can only complicate the lives of all of us," he said.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the smaller Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), also accused Mowlam of undermining trust.
"I think it augurs ill for the talks process as we move into a vital period of those talks in the next fortnight," he said.

Mowlam insisted that the renewed contacts were initiated by Sinn Fein, which is demanding clarification on key issues as a precondition for seeking a new IRA ceasefire which would admit the party to the negotiations six weeks later.

She was speaking less than 24 hours after police found a huge home-made bomb in the staunchly Irish nationalist city of Londonderry which police believe had been assembled by the IRA or an allied group.

Mitchel McLaughlin, the Sinn Fein chairman, told the BBC earlier that the party needed clarification on key topics including the vexed issue of decommissioning or disarming the IRA, which has snarled the talks since their start in June 1996.
He said that further bombs similar to the 300 lb (140 kg) device found hidden in a coal shed on a Catholic estate were inevitable unless Britain eased its entry into the peace talks.

"Unless we bring about a resolution to the conflict, it will happen again", he told BBC radio. He said Britain had to convince Sinn Fein peace talks would not be bogged down by demands that the IRA surrender the weapons it has used in a 28-year-old war against British rule in the province.

McLaughlin's statement held out little hope of an early Irish Republican Army ceasefire which politicians had called for as a response to the Protestant Orange Order's decision last week to scrap four contentious parades through Catholic areas.
The decision meant the Order's "Glorious 12th" anniversary went off in relative peace, despite some clashes in North Belfast between Protestant and Catholic youths.
